F2.Q1: Cut stone flagging — irregular rectangular slabs, mortarless, under a heavy carpet of moss.
F2.Q1_WHY: Dark 1–2px seams enclose slabs of slightly differing tone, e.g. the clean vertical seam at x≈288 running y≈20–130, and the T-junction at (302, 128). The slabs are flat, hard-edged, and read as laid, not as bedrock or packed earth. The warm tan is the torch, not the material: in the unlit left corridor (x 0–180, y 140–290) the identical stone reads grey-blue with a green cast. That's grey stone lit orange.
F2.Q2: The bottom corridor (x≈374–440, heading down off-screen). **Nothing about the ground influenced that** — I picked it off the room's shape, because it's the only opening with a clear "this continues" silhouette. The ground gave me nothing to go on. F2.Q3: No. It is *decorated* as if things happened to it, but nothing localised has happened. It's evenly overgrown, evenly scratched, evenly scuffed — an unbroken statistical average of "old" with no single event anywhere in it.

(2) Moss grows at the same density in the pitch-black left corridor as directly under the torch. (3) The scratch marks are spread at equal density over stone faces, seams and corners alike — including the middle of the 2-tile-wide bottom corridor at (400, 480), which is the one place in frame that should be scoured smooth by four hundred years of a company walking through it.
F2.Q4:
Not NOTHING — three things, and one of them is a hard clone.

- **The diagonal hatch fan.** A splayed set of ~6 pale parallel scratches at 45°. It appears **pixel-identical** at (460, 36) and (524, 228) — normalised correlation 0.99 against itself, versus 0.55 for its own mirror image. Template-matching finds ~48 further instances across the floor, and they nearly all run the same way, lower-left to upper-right. Clearest cluster: (224,68), (308,98), (342,80), (428,134), (490,68), (572,44) — six in the top band alone, all the same angle.
- **A whole tile stamped twice, side by side, at the top of the screen.** The 64px tile at x 310–374 and the one at x 374–438, both y 16–80, are the same art. They are immediate neighbours. Same seam, same moss blob, same hatch, same dark hook-blotch, shifted 64px right. It's the first thing above the figure's head.
- **The moss confetti.** Mid-green blobs of near-identical size scattered at even spacing with no clustering into wall junctions, low points, or damp lines — it reads as noise laid over the floor rather than something growing on it.
F2.Q5: An image that was repeated. 42 floor tiles visible; clustering them after normalising out the lighting, **at least 21 are duplicates of another tile on the same screen**. Four distinct tiles each appear 3–4 times: {(310,16),(374,16),(182,144),(310,208)}; {(502,16),(438,144),(566,144),(502,272)}; {(374,80),(566,80),(502,144),(566,272)}; {(246,16),(182,208),(246,336)}. No rotation, no mirroring, no per-instance variation — every stamp is the raw tile. Half the floor is four pictures.
F2.Q6:
YES. The palette is disciplined, the seams are clean, the moss reads at phone size, and the torch falloff is genuinely good.

Merely competent. Not good. It's a well-drawn tile losing to its own tiling, and the fiction it's supposed to carry — administered, endlessly repaired, four centuries of boots — is nowhere in it. There is not one pin, one rope lashing, one salvaged board, one patch on this floor. It's a ruin, not a workplace.
F2.CULL: Same 64px tile stamped side-by-side at screen top; one scratch motif cloned pixel-exact twice. Reads as wallpaper.
F2.FLIP LIST:
- Break the clone at x 310–438, y 16–80 — that pair of identical adjacent tiles is the single most visible failure in frame; it needs 8–12 distinct floor tiles minimum, plus mirroring/rotation at stamp time.
- Vary the diagonal hatch fan: mirror it, rotate it to at least three angles, and cut its frequency by half. Right now ~48 instances all rake the same direction.
- Break the flat moss field into a gradient — heavy in wall junctions and corners, thinning to bare stone through the corridor mouth at (374–440, 360–440) and along the room's main axis. Moss should mark where feet don't go.
- Add repair to the ground itself: two or three tiles with a driven iron pin, a lashed timber plank over a broken slab, a hide patch. The orcs have held this for four hundred years and have touched nothing you can see.
- Cut one or two cracked/subsided slabs with a real depth offset, placed deliberately rather than scattered, so the eye has a non-repeating landmark to navigate by.

Next thing worth checking: whether the tiler supports per-stamp mirror/rotate at all. If it doesn't, that's the fix that unblocks four of the five items above, and it's cheaper than drawing more tiles.

F1.Q1: I can't tell. Flat tan blocks with dark lines drawn between them. If forced: sandstone or unfired brick. Nothing in the image commits to a material.
F1.Q1_WHY: I sampled every pixel of the walkable area (x 180–628, y 16–400). The entire floor sits at hue 27–28° and saturation 0.49 — one hue, one saturation, only brightness changes. There is no grain, no aggregate, no chip, no fracture face, no edge where one stone is a different stock than its neighbour. The dark lines between blocks (e.g. the long horizontal run at y≈272 spanning x 180–370) are the same brown at lower value, not a different substance. It is a colour, not a material.
F1.Q2:
South, down the corridor at x 372–436 — and **nothing about the ground influenced that.** I picked it because it's the only place the *room shape* changes, and that's geometry, not floor.

The three exits are ground-identical. West (x 0–180, y 145–290), north, and south are the same tiles at the same speckle density with the same hue. The only difference between them is how dark they're drawn, and that's the lantern falloff, not the surface. Walking one way rather than another, I'd learn nothing from what's under my feet. So: effectively random.
F1.Q3: No. It is untouched. Nothing has been dragged across it, dropped on it, worn into it, patched, or spilled. This is the newest thing in the fiction.
F1.Q3_WHY:
I measured dark-speckle density per 64px tile across the whole room. Every tile lands between 0.12 and 0.19 — the tile the figure stands on, the tile in the far corner, the tile at the corridor mouth, all the same. Wear is not uniform; noise is. That flat number is a noise layer, and it's the only "damage" present.

Searching for actual incident, I found three marks total: an eight-pointed dark blob at (355, 255), the same blob again at (430, 415) in the corridor mouth, and again at (147, 232) in the unlit west. Three of one thing, pixel-identical, is not a history.

For a place in continuous heavy use since before records, held by a garrison that repairs everything with rope and driven pins for four hundred years, there is not one pin, one rope-scuff, one board, one dark patch where the traffic goes. The orcs have never walked here.
F1.Q4:
Four things.

1. **Every tile is outlined.** I measured dark-pixel density by position within the 64px tile: 0.34 at the tile's own edge (offset 0), 0.27 at offset 63, and 0.071 in the middle. A 4.5× spike exactly on the boundary, both axes. The mortar draws the game's grid. Once seen at the room's centre it can't be unseen anywhere — the top edge at y≈16, the row at y≈272, the column at x≈436.

2. **The same tile, four times.** Tiles at (x 372, y 80), (x 564, y 80), (x 500, y 144) and (x 564, y 272) are the same image: same jog in the vertical seam, same L-notch, same speckle blobs in the same places. Two other tiles also appear four times each, and six more appear twice. Of 40 visible floor tiles, 24 are duplicates of something else on the same screen.

3. **The blob**, described above — three copies, unshaded, sitting on top of the floor rather than in it.

4. **A prop glyph — two black squares either side of a thin vertical line — appears twice at nearly the same height**: (335, 175) beside the figure and (85, 170) out west. I take that to be an entity rather than floor, so I'm not scoring it, but my eye went to it repeatedly and I'd want to know why there are two.
F1.Q5: Repeated. Three tiles used four times apiece within one phone screen, with no rotation, no mirroring, and no offset to break the match. The masonry snaps to the same 64px lattice as the walls, so the "slabs" are not slabs — they're cells. And every seam is a symmetric dark groove: I measured brightness 4px above versus below every horizontal mortar run (8.07 vs 7.55) and left versus right of every vertical one (7.79 vs 7.57). No side is lit. There is no relief and no light direction. It is a drawing of masonry laid over a grid, not a surface with depth.
F1.Q6:
YES.

Merely competent. The value range is controlled, the lantern falloff is clean, it reads instantly as walkable, and it never fights the sprite. That is the whole of it. It has no point of view about what this place is, and at the size it's played you see the lattice before you see the room.
F1.CULL: Tile grid is drawn on the floor by the mortar, and three tiles repeat four times each per screen.
F1.FLIP LIST:
- Move mortar off the 64px boundary — no seam within 6px of a tile edge; run masonry courses across tile joins so a block can be 1×2 or 2×1 tiles.
- Cut the shared-edge duplication: no tile appears more than twice per screen, and repeats must be mirrored or rotated.
- Replace the uniform speckle with directed wear — brighter, smoother, less-speckled ground along the room's through-lines (corridor mouth at x 372–436 into the room centre), heavier grit and debris in the corners.
- Give the stone a light direction: a one-pixel bright lip on the north/west side of each block and a darker groove on the south/east, so slabs sit proud instead of being outlined.
- Add four hundred years of the garrison at floor level — a driven pin, a rope-worn groove, a salvaged plank bridging a broken slab, one stained patch — placed sparsely, not tiled.

The green zone (zoomed at 215–300 × 10–140) is a single dark teal with a barely-visible lattice under it and three identical green blobs stamped on it; nothing in it says stone, water, or growth.

F4.Q3: _B:** It's old and has been walked on, but nothing has been *done* to it. The stone is worn — faces smoothed, edges of slabs rounded off, seams opened up where mortar has gone. F4.Q1_B: _WHY:** The slabs are visibly different sizes and don't line up: the large one at roughly (255–350, 40–120) is about twice the width of the narrow one at (200–255, 280–370), and seams jog rather than running through. The seams are dark, thin and slightly ragged — mortar gone or never there. The faces carry a fine two-value speckle that reads as grit and pitting rather than noise, and there are lighter patches on individual slabs, like different stone from different sources. The cracks (e.g. the long one at ~(500–600, 250)) run *across* slab faces, not along seams, which is how stone actually fails.
F4.Q5_B: An image that was repeated — but only just, and I had to measure to say it. At a glance it reads as made: slab sizes vary, cracks cross seams, no motif recurs within a screen. F4.Q6_B:
YES. And it is genuinely good — not merely competent. The tell is that the irregularity is *structural*, not noise: slab boundaries ignore the tile grid, damage sits where a floor would actually fail, and the reuse takes measurement to find rather than jumping out. That is real craft.

It is not finished, though. It's good stone and an empty stage.
F4.CULL_B: Floor is spotless — no grime, no debris, no repair anywhere, in a place used continuously for centuries.
F4.RANK:
Not close. A's dirt is a single 48-pixel stamp repeated with up to 98% pixel identity and its grey field is graph paper; B's floor survives the same measurement at ~1% and only fails on one hidden duplicate. B's remaining problem is content — the floor is too clean for the fiction — which is additive work. A's problem is the tile set itself, which is a rebuild.

Watch for: B's cleanliness is the thing that will start to read as wrong once the walls are finished and the room is dressed. Fix the grime and the repairs before adding more props.
